title: Angles need their own statistics: directional analysis of gait coordination, validated against `circular`

dataset.name: WBDS -- a public data set of overground and treadmill walking (Fukuchi et al. 2018)
dataset.record: five subjects (WBDS01-05), treadmill walking; the knee-ankle vector-coding coupling angles (degrees) over one gait cycle (WBDS01: 449 angles)
dataset.citation: Fukuchi CA, Fukuchi RK, Duarte M. A public dataset of overground and treadmill walking kinematics and kinetics in healthy individuals. PeerJ 2018;6:e4640. Data: figshare doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.5722711 (CC-BY 4.0). Vector coding: Needham RA, Naemi R, Chockalingam N. J Biomech 2014.

proposition: An angle is not an ordinary number: 0 and 360 degrees are the same point, so the ordinary mean and standard deviation give nonsense, and directional data need their own statistics. In biomechanics this matters directly -- the vector-coding coupling angle describes how two joints co-vary through a movement, and its circular statistics quantify inter-joint coordination: the mean resultant length R-bar (0-1) is the coordination consistency, and the mean direction is the dominant coordination pattern (in-phase, anti-phase, or one joint dominating). On real WBDS walking, the knee-ankle coupling angles over a gait cycle have mean direction 254 degrees and R-bar = 0.195 (weak but significantly non-uniform, Rayleigh p = 3e-8), and the coordination consistency varies across subjects (R-bar 0.06-0.29). The ecosystem's circularSummary reproduces the canonical R `circular` package to machine precision: the mean resultant length matches exactly (|difference| = 0) and the mean direction to 6x10^-14. The directional statistics the ecosystem reports are, to the bit, the field-standard ones.

claims.statement: mean coordination direction of the knee-ankle coupling angles (degrees), WBDS01
mean resultant length R-bar (coordination consistency, 0-1), the Rayleigh statistic
mean resultant length across all five WBDS subjects (robustness)

validation.reference: The R `circular` package (Agostinelli & Lund) is the canonical implementation of directional statistics. A correct implementation must reproduce its mean direction and mean resultant length. On the real knee-ankle gait coupling angles, circularSummary matches circular::mean.circular and circular::rho.circular to machine precision (R-bar |diff| = 0, mean direction |diff| = 5.7e-14). The Rayleigh test agrees on strong significance (both p ~ 3e-8); its p-value is an asymptotic approximation whose higher-order series differ slightly between the two libraries.
validation.data: REAL -- WBDS (Fukuchi et al. 2018, PeerJ; figshare 5722711, CC-BY 4.0), five subjects of treadmill walking; knee-ankle vector-coding coupling angles
validation.note: The reproducible finding is the machine-precision agreement on the definitional circular statistics: mean direction |diff| = 5.7e-14, R-bar |diff| = 0. HONEST scope: (1) the mean direction and R-bar are exactly-defined, so they match the `circular` package to the bit; (2) the Rayleigh test p-value is an ASYMPTOTIC APPROXIMATION -- PhysioCore::rayleighTest and circular::rayleigh.test use slightly different higher-order series, so they agree on strong significance (op p = 3.16e-8 vs circular 3.66e-8) but are NOT bit-identical, and this is reported, not claimed as an exact match; (3) the coupling angles over a full gait cycle are broadly distributed (R-bar ~ 0.20, a weak but significant directional bias), and the coordination consistency genuinely varies across subjects (R-bar 0.06-0.29) -- a real between-subject spread, not noise; (4) run_simulation = FALSE (deterministic).

open_questions.q: R-bar and the mean coupling direction are the raw material of coordination analysis: comparing them between limbs, between groups (via the Watson-Williams test, watsonWilliamsTest), or across the gait cycle (phase-binned coupling-angle distributions, the standard coordination-variability analysis) would turn these validated directional statistics into a coordination study. The between-subject R-bar spread (0.06-0.29) already hints at individual coordination signatures worth testing. Documented, not escalated.
